title: Leading consonants: อักษรนำ

slides.heading: The letter written in front that you never hear
body: Ten letters that cannot spell a rising tone or a low tone alone.
Thai's answer: write another consonant in front of them.
Three places you have already met this, and one rule underneath all three.

slides.heading: Pen and paper
body: Real paper, a real pen.
Today you write the worked examples, one by one.
Both halves of the name, out loud, every time.

slides.heading: Ten letters that cannot be written with a rising tone
body: ง ญ ณ น ม ย ร ล ว ฬ are the sonorants: the ten letters you can hold and hum.
Every one of them is low class, and none has a high or mid class twin the way ค has ข.
A low class letter on its own can reach mid, falling and high tone, and that is all. Rising tone and low tone are simply not spellable on it.
Thai solves this by putting another letter in front. That front letter is not there to be heard. It is there to be a class.

slides.heading: The rule, once
body: A mid or high class consonant written directly in front of a sonorant leads it, and hands its class to the syllable the sonorant opens.
Nothing else changes. The vowel, the final and the live or dead reading are whatever the written syllable says they are; only the class comes from outside.
Hold it as a strong tendency rather than a law. A small number of words keep the second letter's own class, and one of them is coming up.
Everything below is that one sentence meeting three different first letters, rather than three separate rules.

slides.heading: First letter ห, and you do not hear it
body: หมด (mòt) is finished, หลง (lǒng) is to be lost, หนัง (nǎng) is a film, หญิง (yǐng) is a woman, หมอ (mǎaw) is a doctor, หรอก (ràawk) softens a denial.
There is no h in any of them. ห in this position is written and never spoken.
Any of the ten may follow it, and new words still take it, so treat this as open.

slides.heading: First letter อ, four words, no more
body: อย่า (yàa) is don't. อยู่ (yùu) is to stay. อย่าง (yàang) is a kind or sort. อยาก (yàak) is to want. That is the complete list.
อ in front of ย is silent here, exactly as ห is.
There is no fifth word and no fifth is coming. Read ยาก and ยาว as the low class ย they are, because nothing precedes them.

slides.heading: Any other mid or high first letter, and you do hear it
body: สวัสดี (sà-wàt-dii) at rank nine is this branch, and so are ขนาด (khà-nàat), ตลอด (dtà-làawt), สงบ (sà-ngòp), สมัย (sà-mǎi), ผลิต (phà-lìt) and ถนน (thà-nǒn).
Here the first letter keeps its own sound. It takes the short a of a consonant that will not fit, and becomes a light syllable ahead of the main one.
ตลก (dtà-lòk), ขนม (khà-nǒm), ขยาย (khà-yǎai), ตลาด (dtà-làat) and ฉลาด (chà-làat) are the same shape. This branch is wide open and you will meet it daily.

slides.prompt: หมด begins with ห and ตลก begins with ต. In one of them the first letter is spoken and in the other it is not. What is the same about the two words?

answers: In both, the letter in front is the one the tone is worked out from, and the letter after it is not.
Spoken or not spoken: that is all that separates one branch from the next.

slides.heading: When the first letter is simply the initial
body: สนใจ (sǒn-jai) puts ส in front of น and is one syllable rather than two: both letters share a short o, and ส is simply the initial.
Count syllables the shorter way first. Only when a letter cannot be read into the syllable beside it does it become a leader.
And a low class first letter never leads at all. It has no class the sonorant does not already have, so นคร is ná-khaawn with two ordinary syllables.

slides.heading: And one word that keeps its own class
body: สมาชิก (sà-maa-chík) is a member, and it splits into a light first syllable and then the rest, the way the whole lesson has trained you to split.
The middle syllable keeps the class it was born with, so it comes out flat where the rule predicts a rising tone.
Derive the reading, then let a dictionary overrule you on the few words that go their own way.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: Chest, mouse, snake closing the first syllable.
Then the tiger's letter, a roof vowel, and the prop behind it.
Two tones to work out. Out loud before you turn it over.

slides.heading: That one
body: **หนังสือ** — a book.
Both syllables rise. The first gets there through the letter in front of it.
The second gets there on its own, because the tiger already lives uphill.

slides.heading: And this one, which looks like the last trap
body: It opens with the same two letters as the word on the counting slide.
Look at what follows the second letter.
Out loud before you turn it over.

slides.heading: That one
body: **สนามบิน** — an airport.
The second letter has its own vowel and ending, so the two cannot share a syllable.
Read past the second letter before you split a word.

slides.prompt: หมด and มด are both real words, both read with a short o and a d that stops the air. Why do they not have the same tone?

answers: มด (mót) is high tone, because ม is low class and the syllable is short and dead.
หมด (mòt) is low tone, because the ห in front makes the reading a high class one.

slides.heading: That is the required course
body: Three branches, one rule, and a tendency rather than a law.
An unfamiliar word: split it, find the class, find the ending, say the tone.
One optional lesson remains: the ten Thai digits.
